newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-BAe sees Anglo-German-French defence group.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BAe sees Anglo-German-French defence group.

text.p: The managing director of British Aerospace Plc told a French parliamentary committee that he envisaged a combination of his company, Germany's Daimler-Aerospace and Aerospatiale-Dassault to create European giant.

In minutes of the Tuesday meeting, published on Wednesday, John Weston said such a grouping was "the strict minimum to create a European company" and added that Italian, Spanish and Swedish firms were also essential partners.
He told the committee, which met behind closed doors, that it was difficult to merge four, five or six companies at the same time but he said a step-by-step approach was possible.
Weston has been campaigning for a large European aerospace group for some months.
He said that while the United States defence industry was powerful and increasingly concentrated, Europe had been slow in adapting.
"Weston said that the consolidation of the European industry is not only urgent, but already overdue," the minutes said.
Weston said that the French state's 100-percent stake in Aerospatiale and 50 percent stake in Dassault Aviation, which are slated to merge, would be an obstacle to such a wide-ranging merger.

"It would be very difficult for the management of BAe to propose to their shareholders to exchange the control of 100 percent of their company against a fraction of a European company in which a state would have a major stake," Weston was indirectly quoted as saying.
He envisaged a shell company in which the partners could have a stake and transfer assets at a later stage.
A DASA spokesman in Munich said on Wednesday a European merger would be a "desirable long-term goal" in the light of the United States mergers but "in the short-term unrealistic."

Weston made clear that BAe had no plans to leave the Airbus Industrie consortium and despite its recent deal with Lockheed-Martin on the JSF fighter plane, the company had no transatlantic preference.
In civil aerospace, the planned transformation of Airbus into a joint stock company was an urgent answer to an increasingly competitive market.

He said that the status of Aerospatiale as a state-owned company was not an obstacle to the transformation of Airbus but could be a blocking element in the next stage of a block merger of the parent groups which would only be possible if all companies were private.

"The elimination of industrial duplication and performance improvement are key factors behind the success of the project because only (good) financial performance will allow such a long-term development," Weston was quoted as saying.

Manfred Bischoff, chairman of Daimler Aerospace (DASA), was also separately heard by the commission on Tuesday. He said that a new phase was needed in which European joint-ventures became single European companies.

"It seems that the margin for reaction in Europe is getting smaller at the same time that the international competition is increasing and a new technological and economic breath should push the U.S. industry towards selling in Europe," he was quoted as saying.

On Airbus, Bischoff said that it should become a company with a single management which runs all the assets and have a single balance sheet which represents all its activities. "That is the single solution to take up the gauntlet thrown by Boeing," he said. Bischoff added that the Airbus headquarters could remain in Toulouse.
Aerospatiale and Dasa have 38 percent each in Airbus. British Aerospace Plc has 20 percent and CASA of Spain four percent.
